children: Bangladesh's garment factory owners's reported opening offer of about 15% would leave workers poorer than in 2023. An over nine hour marathon meeting ended without a deal between the owners and workers's representatives on November 23, 2026.

After nine and a half hours of talks the newly constituted so called wage board adjourned until 2pm on November 24. Its chairman, Syed Azad Subhani, would not disclose the owners's exact figure officially but said a decision could come at an extended meeting,
The Daily Star
reported.
Babul Akhter, who sits on the board for the workers, said the two sides were still far apart. Subhani told reporters only that the offer was above BDT14,500 ($116) a month, according to
AFP
. Akhter has asked for BDT32,000, against a current floor of BDT12,500.
Industry leaders told
Reuters

that owners could go to about 15%. A 15% rise takes the floor to roughly BDT14,375, close to the BDT14,300 two leaders of the Bangladesh Garment Manufacturers and Exporters Association (BGMEA) had earlier given
The Daily Star

. Consumer prices, however, have risen 28.7% since the current minimum was set in November 2023. An award of 15% would buy about 11% less than the wage it replaces, which helps explain why a month of strikes and road blockades has not burnt itself out.
Opening bids are not final
Past rounds of negotiations suggest the factory owners's figure is a starting point. In 2018 the owners opened at BDT6,360 and the floor was set at BDT8,000, 26% higher,
The Daily Star
reported at the time. In 2023 they opened at BDT10,400 and ended at BDT12,500, a 20% climb. The same margins applied to this year's offer would give BDT17,400-18,300.
A wage board source told the Bangladeshi news site
TOB News

that employers want to hold the minimum below BDT16,500, while Akhter is trying to secure at least BDT17,500, squarely within that range. Simply restoring the 2023 purchasing power of the current wage would need about BDT16,100, so the owners's private ceiling barely clears inflation and the workers' fallback offers a real gain of roughly 9%.
Who pays

The unrest has already cost more than the gap between the two sides. A BGMEA survey found that 317 factories lost about $428mn of production between November 1 and 18, and buyers moved orders worth some $254mn to other countries,
Reuters
reported.

The BDT1,000 a month separating the reported positions would cost about $385mn a year even if every one of the sector's 4mn workers were paid at the minimum. That is less than the production lost in 18 days of protest.

Buyers say they will share the bill. Sixteen brands in the Action, Collaboration, Transformation (ACT) initiative, among them H&M Group, Inditex, Primark, Next and PVH Corp, called for an urgent and meaningful increase in a joint statement on November 19. 'In line with our ACT commitments, we will work with our suppliers so that minimum wage increases and negotiated wage increases are appropriately incorporated into purchasing prices,' they said.

If they keep that promise, the owners' main argument against a bigger award weakens. The government has already tried to cool tempers with subsidised rice for garment workers, the board's chairman has been touring factories, and US brands want yearly wage reviews. The new rate is meant to take effect in December, which leaves the board days rather than weeks to close the gap.

title: Bangladesh garment factory owners's wage offer would leave workers poorer
